lesson.title: From Statistic to Statement
lesson.summary: A goodness-of-fit conclusion turns a chi-square statistic and P-value into a properly hedged sentence about the original claim, without overclaiming what reject or fail to reject actually proves.
lesson.body:
Computing a chi-square statistic and reading off a P-value is only half the job. A goodness-of-fit conclusion has to translate that number back into a sentence about the original claim, using the same careful three-part structure as any other significance test: compare the P-value to the significance level, state a decision about the null hypothesis, and restate that decision in the context of the problem.

Return to the candy color example. The hypotheses were built around the company's claim: H0 is that the true color distribution of all bags matches the company's stated percentages, 30% brown, 20% yellow, 20% red, 10% orange, 10% green, 10% blue, and Ha is that the true distribution differs from the claim in at least one color. The sample gave X squared equals 4.30 with 5 degrees of freedom, 6 colors minus 1. A chi-square distribution with 5 degrees of freedom has a median value of about 4.35, and since our statistic of 4.30 sits just barely below that median, the P-value comes out just above 0.50, roughly 0.51 from technology.

Compare that P-value to a standard significance level such as alpha equals 0.05: 0.51 is far larger than 0.05, so we fail to reject H0. Stated in context: we do not have convincing evidence that the true color distribution of this candy differs from the company's claim. Notice the careful phrasing. Failing to reject H0 does not prove the company's claim is exactly correct, it only means this sample's observed counts were not surprising enough, under the assumption that the claim is true, to rule the claim out. A different sample from the same bags could look somewhat different just by chance.

It helps to picture the other outcome too. Suppose the counts had instead produced a much larger statistic, say X squared equals 15, with the same 5 degrees of freedom. The P-value would then fall below 0.01, comfortably under 0.05, and the conclusion would flip: convincing evidence that the true color distribution differs from the company's claim in at least one color. Even then, the test itself does not identify which color is the culprit. For that, you go back to the individual observed minus expected, squared, over expected terms computed in the previous chapter. In our actual data, green contributed the most, 2.50 of the total 4.30, which is a hint, though not proof on its own, that green candies were showing up more often than the claim predicted.
